results.title: Solo Leveling Season 2 Was a Second Awakening For the Series and a Wake-Up Call For the Anime Industry
results.author: Brett Cardaro
highlights:
By the end of Season 2, though, it officially revealed its true power as one of the biggest anime in the world, and deservedly so. As popular as Solo Leveling has become by the end of Season 2, it’s likely the series will be more divisive than the first season ever was. Solo Leveling Season 2 has unapologetically embraced its identity as a pure power fantasy whose main draw is intense, beautifully animated action, which won’t be for everyone. The occasional tinge of horror, a subtle blooming romance, or Jinwoo's inner conflicts are all just inessential extras. Now that Sung Jinwoo has become one of the strongest Hunters on the planet, Solo Leveling Season 2 sought to show him off in all his edgy, anti-hero glory, and it has paid off.

...

Solo Leveling Season 2 relies on the source material just as much as the first season and does an excellent job faithfully adapting the original story. While some scenes were inevitably cut, very few were of major consequence, and they were often replaced in the long run with anime-only additions that either expanded on the characters or refocused on another vital plot thread. For example, the scenes involving Esil in Solo Leveling Season 2, Episode 8 that were cut to hasten the pacing of the Return to the Demon’s Castle Arc also helped condense the essential beats of her personal growth into a more compact package, which ironically made her feel like more of a focal point. Of course, a big reason behind several omitted manhwa scenes was simply to get to the action sooner.

...

While the inevitable draw of Solo Leveling is the combat, not every single episode of the second season was peak action. Solo Leveling Season 2 has plenty of slowdowns via episodes meant to build the story and characters. In truth, actionless episodes tended to be the least interesting. The most notable exception is the now infamous Solo Leveling Season 2, Episode 9, which also went on to be the season’s most divisive. After all the buildup, Solo Leveling does a great job of having viewers sit with Jinwoo in the moment that

...

While certain aspects of Solo Leveling Season 2’s storyline were divisive for the general anime fandom, one thing that can’t be denied is that its animation and action were the absolute best in the Winter 2025 season. Dragon Ball DAIMA and Shangri La Frontier also delivered some amazing fights, but no series was able to consistently bring the heat throughout the season like Solo Leveling. A-1 Pictures understood the assignment and continuously cooked up absolute peak animation in all the season's biggest fights. Even in minor conflicts, such as the A-Rank Hunter’s Guild strike team’s fight against Kargalagan’s High Orcs, or the sparring match between the S Ranks of Japan and South Korea, the animation and choreography were always phenomenal and on-par with the best fights of the majority of its competitors.

...

Solo Leveling’s manhwa is all about flashy imagery, while the story in the light novel emphasizes Jinwoo’s nonchalant attitude in the face of overwhelming threats to make him look like the coolest possible hero. Somehow, Solo Leveling Season 2 made most of Jinwoo’s fights even more intense than the manhwa did, and Jinwoo ended up becoming synonymous with the term “aura farming” due to how well the anime captured his coolness, as depicted in the light novel. Solo Leveling' s anime adaptation is by no means a replacement for either the manhwa or light novel, as both versions of the story have their own merits. But as of the second season, Solo Leveling’s anime is emerging as the definitive adaptation of the story, and that’s largely due to how incredibly well it has elevated the action.

It’s not just the action alone that is elevating the anime above the manhwa. The Solo Leveling anime is developing its own identity more and more with each season, with a more humanized Jinwoo and characters who are given more development than their source material counterparts. Cha Haein was a character who fans constantly criticized for being shallow in the source material, but the anime has actively continued to add scenes of her in nearly every episode to make her relationship with Jinwoo feel more fulfilling. It’s not exactly working miracles, but there’s no denying that the Haein in the anime is a far more nuanced character than she was in the manhwa, and she's not the only one.

...

Solo Leveling’s second season isn’t perfect, and it won’t be for everyone. All the hype around Solo Leveling’s second season put it in the interesting situation of garnering constant comparison to other series, and that’s to be expected. Solo Leveling doesn’t have the deepest story, and anyone approaching it hoping for strong character development or emotional romance will be disappointed. That’s not to say it’s an entirely shallow series (Solo Leveling Season 3 will help prove that), but an emotional narrative was never its strength, even in the manhwa.

## The “Season 1 / Season 2” Manhwa Labels Are Not Anime Seasons

This trips up almost everyone coming from the anime. The Korean publisher split the manhwa into “Season 1” (chapters 1–98) and “Season 2” (chapters 99–179).

These are publishing labels, not story breaks. There is no gap at chapter 99, no recap, no tonal shift. The story runs straight through. And they do not line up with the anime’s seasons, which end at different points entirely.

| Label | Covers | What it actually means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manhwa “Season 1” | Chapters 1–98 | Publisher volume grouping |
| Manhwa “Season 2” | Chapters 99–179 | Publisher volume grouping |
| Anime Season 1 | ~Chapters 1–45 | 12 episodes |
| Anime Season 2 | ~Chapters 45–110 | 13 episodes |

...

Season 2 ended with the Jeju Island arc, around chapter 110 of the manhwa.

...

### The manhwa: the definitive version

Redice Studio’s art established the visual identity of the entire franchise — the character designs, the shadow soldiers, the look of the gates. When the anime adapted the series, it adapted the manhwa’s visual language, not the novel’s descriptions.

It also trims. Some novel content is condensed or dropped, and a few sequences are restructured. For most readers this is an improvement in pace rather than a loss.

### The anime: motion, sound, and patience

A-1 Pictures’ adaptation is faithful and unusually well resourced. Around 220,000 animation frames were produced across the first two seasons, and Hiroyuki Sawano’s score does heavy lifting in the fight scenes.

The trade-off is obvious: it is incomplete and will stay that way for years. The anime also reduces internal monologue, conveying Jinwoo’s thinking visually instead — which works, but means you lose detail the novel readers have.
